findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema is built with bogus computed keys and strips every field except access_token
findings.body: The schema is declared as `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), [z.string().toString()]: z.number(), [z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional() })`. The computed keys evaluate `ZodString.toString()` / `ZodOptional.toString()`, which both produce the same literal string (`"[object Object]"`), so the resulting schema is just `{ access_token: string, "[object Object]": unknown? }`. The intended behaviour ("assume any property with a number is the expiry" and "allow other properties") is not implemented at all. Worse, because `z.object` strips unknown keys by default, parsing a credential-sync response discards `expires_in`/`expiry_date`/`refresh_token`, so callers that merge `tokenResponse.data` into the stored key (office365calendar, zoomvideo) end up with no expiry at all — the token is treated as permanently expired and refreshed on every request, and zoom computes `expiry_date = Date.now() + NaN`.

findings.title: Injecting the literal string "refresh_token" overwrites valid stored refresh tokens
findings.body: When the parsed response has no `refresh_token`, the function sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. Several callers spread the parsed data over the existing credential key and persist it, e.g. `packages/app-store/office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` does `o365AuthCredentials = { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }` and writes it to the DB. Microsoft legitimately omits `refresh_token` on some refresh responses (the schema marks it optional), so the user's real refresh token is replaced in the database by the useless string "refresh_token" and the integration breaks permanently until re-installed. The same happens for zoomvideo, where `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token` is persisted.

findings.title: Google credential key is overwritten with the zod safeParse wrapper object
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the result of `schema.safeParse(...)`, i.e. `{ success: true, data: {...} }`, but the result is assigned to `key` and written straight to the DB (`prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`). Previously the code stored `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)` (the credential object itself). After the first token refresh every Google Calendar credential will be stored as `{"success":true,"data":{...}}`, which no longer satisfies `googleCredentialSchema`, so subsequent constructions of GoogleCalendarService throw and the calendar connection is broken for the user.

findings.title: Credential-sync branch returns a fetch Response while callers expect provider-specific shapes
findings.body: In the sync branch the helper returns the raw `fetch` `Response`, but the wrapped `refreshFunction` of most callers returns something completely different: google returns a Gaxios response (caller reads `res.data.access_token`), hubspot returns a parsed `HubspotToken` (caller reads `.expiresIn` and stores the object as the credential key), zoho-bigin and zohocrm return an axios response (callers read `tokenInfo.data.error` / `tokenInfo.data.access_token`). With app-credential syncing enabled these callers will read `undefined` off the `Response`, throw TypeErrors, compute `NaN` expiry dates, or persist a serialized `Response` as the credential key. The helper must normalise the sync response (await `response.json()`) into the same shape the refresh function returns, or each caller must be adapted.

findings.title: Credential-sync request is unauthenticated and its status is never checked
findings.body: The POST to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` with no shared secret/signature header (unlike the inbound webhook, which verifies `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`), so the self-hoster's endpoint has no way to tell that the request really came from Cal.com — anybody who knows the URL can harvest access tokens for arbitrary user ids if the endpoint trusts the caller. In addition the response status is never checked, so a 4xx/5xx body is passed to the token parsers as if it were a token response, producing confusing downstream failures instead of a clear error.

findings.title: `prisma` is used but never imported in salesforce CalendarService
findings.body: The newly added code calls `prisma.credential.update(...)` inside `getClient`, but this file has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. This is a compile error (and a `ReferenceError` at runtime if type-checking is bypassed), so every Salesforce booking/calendar operation fails as soon as the service is instantiated.

findings.title: Salesforce connection still uses the old access token after refreshing
findings.body: `getClient` now performs a refresh_token exchange and persists the new token, but the `jsforce.Connection` is still created with `accessToken: credentialKey.access_token` (the stale value read from the credential before refreshing) and `instanceUrl: credentialKey.instance_url`. The refresh is therefore pointless: if the stored access token was expired, every Salesforce API call still fails. The newly parsed `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token` / `instance_url` should be used.

findings.title: Salesforce token is refreshed unconditionally on every service instantiation
findings.body: `getClient` issues a refresh_token request to `login.salesforce.com` and a `credential.update` write every time a `SalesforceCalendarService` is constructed, with no expiry check on the stored token. Since the service is constructed per booking/availability operation this adds a blocking round trip plus a DB write to every request and will hit Salesforce's refresh-token rate limits on busy instances.

findings.title: Error detection via `response.statusText !== "OK"` is unreliable
findings.body: The refresh result is validated with `if (response.statusText !== "OK") throw ...`. `statusText` is an empty string for HTTP/2 responses (undici does not synthesize a reason phrase), so a perfectly successful refresh can be rejected with an `HttpError` whose message is empty, while a non-2xx response with reason phrase "OK" would be accepted. Use `response.ok` / `response.status` instead.

findings.title: Zoho Bigin passes a credential id where a user id is expected
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` passes `credentialId` as the third argument, which the helper uses as `calcomUserId` in the credential-sync request body. The self-hosted endpoint will receive a credential id instead of the Cal.com user id, so it will either return the wrong user's tokens or fail. `refreshAccessToken` should receive and forward `credential.userId`.

findings.title: Zoom sends appSlug "zoomvideo", which is not the app's slug
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoomvideo", credential.userId)` sends `appSlug=zoomvideo`, but the Zoom app's slug used everywhere else (callback stores `appId: "zoom"`, and the new `/api/webhook/app-credential` endpoint looks the app up with `prisma.app.findUnique({ where: { slug } })`) is `zoom`. A self-hoster keying off `appSlug` will not be able to map the sync request back to the credential the webhook created, so Zoom credential syncing silently fails.

findings.title: Webex refresh still validated with the strict provider schema, so credential sync cannot work
findings.body: Webex was switched to `refreshOAuthTokens` but the response is still validated with `webexRefreshedTokenSchema.safeParse(...)`, which requires an exact `scope` literal, `token_type: "Bearer"`, `refresh_token` and `refresh_token_expires_in`. A self-hosted sync endpoint is documented to return only the access token and expiry, so the parse always fails and `refreshAccessToken` rejects with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". Either use `parseRefreshTokenResponse` here (as done for zoom/office365) or don't wire Webex into the sync flow.

findings.title: Webhook handler has no method guard and throws raw errors on malformed input
findings.body: The handler accepts any HTTP verb (GET/DELETE included) and uses `schema.parse(req.body)` plus `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` without try/catch. A malformed body, a payload encrypted with the wrong key, or non-JSON plaintext results in an unhandled exception and a 500 with a stack trace instead of a 400/422 with a useful message. Restrict to POST and use `safeParse` / wrap the decryption in a try/catch.

findings.title: Updating synced credentials does not clear the `invalid` flag
findings.body: When a credential already exists the handler only writes `key`. Credentials that were previously marked `invalid: true` (e.g. google/zoom/webex set this on `invalid_grant`) stay invalid after fresh keys are pushed in, so Cal.com keeps treating the connection as broken even though valid tokens were just synced. The update should also reset `invalid: false`.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with a non-constant-time `!==` and header may be an array
findings.body: The shared secret check uses a plain string inequality, which short-circuits on the first differing byte and is therefore vulnerable to timing analysis; use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers. Additionally `req.headers[name]` can be `string[]` when the header is sent twice, in which case the comparison always fails and legitimate callers get a 403 with no explanation.

findings.title: findFirst + update can leave duplicate credentials out of sync
findings.body: Because the lookup is `findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })`, when a user has more than one credential row for the same app (which happens for several apps that historically allowed duplicates) only one row is updated; the stale rows keep their old keys and may still be selected by other code paths (`findFirst` is used in several adapters). Two concurrent webhook deliveries can also both see no credential and create two rows. Consider a unique constraint or an `updateMany`/transaction.

findings.title: No tests for the new credential webhook or the token-parsing helpers
findings.body: This PR adds a publicly reachable endpoint that decrypts a payload and writes third-party OAuth credentials for arbitrary user ids, plus two new shared helpers (`parseRefreshTokenResponse`, `refreshOAuthTokens`) used by ~10 app integrations, with no unit tests. Basic tests covering secret mismatch, unknown user/app, bad ciphertext, create-vs-update behaviour, and the token-schema fallback would have caught the schema and response-shape defects noted elsewhere in this review.
